newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain sees stability pact as way to boost jobs.
newsitem.headline: Spain sees stability pact as way to boost jobs.

text.p: Spain, which suffers from Europe's highest unemployment rate, said on Tuesday a pact assuring fiscal discipline after the launch of Europe's single currency was the best way to create new jobs.
Spanish Economy Secretary Cristobal Montoro brushed aside concerns of some EU partners that a stability plan to be enforced after the euro's launch would cost jobs.
EU partners including Britain and France have both proposed job creation schemes in recent days, with measures such as giving aid to small and medium firms to provide more jobs.

France, in particular, has spoken out for a more social Europe and requested time to think over the stability pact, dashing expectations it would be approved at a European summit in Amsterdam mid-month.
But for Spain, which has already committed itself to the EU pact with the approval of its three-year convergence plan, the pact is the solution and not the problem.
"(The stability pact) isn't causing any difficulties for society..it favours steady, stable growth with job creation," Economy Secretary Montoro said on Tuesday.
"Spain wants to be part of the euro, we are convinced this is the best way to solve economic problems," he said.
On Monday, Spain's Labour ministry said 57,866 new jobs were created in May alone. Between March 1996 and March 1997, some 300,000 new jobs were created.
In May, 13.26 percent of the working population was registered as unemployed, while a household survey showed 21.49 percent out of work in the first quarter.
But far from considering convergence and fiscal discipline an impediment to employment, Spain considers a timely and a strong euro the best way to dent unemployment.
"Nobody in Europe intends to delay EMU. The euro has a calendar that no one has questioned and furthermore its delay would be politically impossible," Montoro said.
"France has only asked for time because its parliament has not yet been formed," Montoro said.
Accelerating growth and declining inflation should also help boost job creation.

In the first quarter of the year Spanish gross domestic product (GDP) rose 2.9 percent over the same period a year ago. The Economy Ministry expects inflation to moderate to 1.5 percent from April's 1.7 percent.
Spain already meets three out of the five Maastricht criteria on inflation, currency stability and long-term interest rates. Debt is expected to be excessive, but to decline as required.
The budget deficit is seen hitting the required target of three percent of GDP.
Budget Secretary Jose Folgado forecast that from July the budget deficit would narrow on a year-on-year basis by some 40 percent by the end of the year.
"These data are the Spanish passport to enter EMU," Montoro said.
